stem: [ATP] The following steps are ensured when preparing crystals of pure copper sulphate (CuSO4.5H2O) from an impure sample of blue vitriol: A few drops of dilute sulphuric acid are added to the aqueous solution; The filtrate should be evaporated only up to the crystallisation point. The purpose of adding dilute sulphuric acid is to

options.A: breakdown copper sulphate into its ions.
options.B: prevent the hydrolysis of copper sulphate.
options.C: cause the decomposition of copper sulphate.
options.D: remove impurities present in copper sulphate.

sloText: Explain the practical precautions in salt crystallization including suppressing cation hydrolysis;
explanation: Copper(II) sulphate in hot aqueous solution undergoes slight hydrolysis: Cu2+ + 2H2O ⇌ Cu(OH)2 + 2H+, which can precipitate cloudy basic copper salt and dull the crystal transparency. Adding a few drops of dilute H2SO4 suppresses this hydrolysis, maintaining clear, pure blue crystals.

option_feedback.reason: Water already dissolves and dissociates the salt into ions.
Correct. Dilute H2SO4 shifts the hydrolysis equilibrium backward, preventing turbidity and basic salt precipitation.
Acid prevents decomposition rather than causing it.
Insoluble impurities are removed by filtration, not by acid addition.

stem: [ATP] If heating is exceeded (beyond the crystallisation point) to dryness, then this causes: I. disappearance of blue colour, II. loss of water of crystallisation, III. disappearance of the compound, IV. loss of turbidity from the solution
sloText: Describe the effect of overheating hydrated salts to complete dryness;
explanation: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4·5H2O) is bright blue. Overheating to dryness drives off the five molecules of coordinated water of crystallization, converting it into white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate powder (CuSO4). Hence, I and II occur.

option_feedback.reason: Correct. Overheating removes water of crystallization and turns blue hydrated crystals into white anhydrous powder.
The compound does not disappear; it remains as white solid powder.
Turbidity is not an indicator here.
Statement III is false.

sloText: Identify the components of an electroplating cell and distinguish from galvanic cells;
explanation: Electroplating is conducted in a single electrolytic bath with a shared electrolyte solution where ions move directly between the anode and cathode. Salt bridges are used exclusively in two-compartment voltaic/galvanic cells to connect separate half-cells.

sloText: Infer relative electrolyte strength (non, weak, strong) from conductivity bulb brightness;
explanation: Cell X produces no light -> Non-electrolyte (Ethanol, which dissolves as neutral molecules). Cell Y produces dim light -> Weak electrolyte (Acetic acid, which ionizes only partially in water). Cell Z produces bright light -> Strong electrolyte (Potassium chloride, which dissociates completely into mobile K+ and Cl- ions).

option_feedback.reason: KCl is a strong electrolyte and would produce bright light in Cell X.
Ethanol is a non-electrolyte and would produce no light in Cell Y.
Acetic acid would produce dim light in Cell X, not zero light.
Correct. Ethanol (non-electrolyte), acetic acid (weak electrolyte), and KCl (strong electrolyte).
